Observations of some variable X-ray sources within the Milky Way's center that have shown no outbursts in over a decade have led some researchers to suggest a significant population of stellar mass black holes in the region. A crucial aspect of the theory that these sources are actually black holes is the claim that neutron star binaries with low masses exhibit recurring X-ray bursts within short intervals. This study contradicts that idea by revealing that about half of the known LMXBs, featuring a neutron star as the primary component, exhibit outburst recurrence times exceeding 10 years when detected by the MAXI telescope. Moreover, to reconcile the total population of neutron star binaries with observed and radio pulsar populations within the Milky Way, researchers find that a significant majority of these binaries have recurrence times exceeding a century for outbursts visible to the MAXI telescope and most remain undiscovered. The findings support the possibility that some variable X-ray sources within the Milky Way's center might be neutron star binaries rather than black holes, thus offering an alternative explanation for the nature of the quiescent X-ray binaries observed in the region.

Bipartite graphs depicting connections between distinct groups of objects have numerous practical applications, and their visualization often takes the form of a 2-tier layout where corresponding entities are aligned horizontally across two parallel lines, connected by lines representing relationships between them. The task of reducing edge crossings within these visualizations can be computationally intensive, yet might not always guarantee sufficiently low crossings levels to maintain the visualization's clarity. In contrast, an approach has been developed to remove edge crossings by splitting specific nodes, targeting the minimum number required to yield an edge-free (planar) graph. The question of determining if an edge-free representation exists after breaking at most a specified number of nodes remains tractable in relation to that number. The purpose of this paper has been to develop an algorithm that solves this problem in a time-proportional manner to the specified limit. The algorithm's effectiveness has been demonstrated by applying it to various large-scale graphs, compared to alternative methods for comparison. The paper's contributors have also created an available dataset for public use.

In 1930, mathematician K. Menger developed an interest in the concept of metric spaces, specifically in the context of angular metrics. Building upon this foundation, he introduced the notion of angular metric spaces, which can be thought of as partially ordering points within a given region. The structure of these spaces is defined through the angular distance between points, which in turn gives rise to a partial order. The ordered sets resulting from this structure are then termed angle spaces. Menger's interest in these sets led him to pose several problems, two of which remain unresolved to this day. The first problem involves determining whether the real numbers, when viewed as an ordered set of angular distance, are comparable. The second problem asks whether the ordering relationship in these sets can be fully linearized under certain distance metrics. In this paper, we provide solutions to both of these problems. The real numbers, when considered as an ordered set of angular distance, do not give rise to a linear order. However, we do observe a linear order when we shift to negative degrees of the Lebesgue measure on the real line. Additionally, we find that the ordering relationship in these sets can be fully linearized when we apply the inverse relation to the usual linear order of the real numbers. The solutions presented involve using forcing arguments in the context of infinite subsets of the real line, as well as using measure theory to define a linear order among the ordering relationships within these sets. The paper concludes by exploring the implications of these solutions within the realm of angle spaces, specifically in regards to coexistence, preservation under extension, and linearization.
